title: Insurify Projects the Average US Home Insurance Premium Will Reach $3,057 in 2026, a Fifth Straight Annual Rise, With Florida at $8,458 and California Facing the Largest Percentage Increase at 16%
summary: Insurify projects the average US homeowners premium will rise 4% to $3,057 in 2026 after a 12% rise to $2,948 in 2025, with Florida the most expensive state at $8,458, California the largest percentage increase at 16% and Nebraska the largest dollar increase at $532, driven by severe storms, wildfire losses and rebuilding costs.
description:
Home insurance prices in the United States are expected to rise again in 2026. That is the central finding of a projection by Insurify, an online insurance comparison company, which was reported by Insurance Journal and Claims Journal on March 18, 2026. This article is based on Insurify's published projections. It is important to be clear about what the figures are: they are modelled estimates built from the company's own quote data and public rate filings, not official government statistics, and they describe a standardized policy rather than what any particular household pays.

The national picture

Insurify projects that the average annual premium for a standard homeowners policy will reach $3,057 by the end of 2026. That is an increase of about 4% from a 2025 average of $2,948, which Insurify says was itself 12% higher than the $2,636 average at the end of 2024. Insurify describes 2026 as the fifth consecutive year of rising rates. It also says average premiums have risen 46% since 2021, about three times the 16% increase in consumer prices over the same period, and that the average has increased by more than $900 over that time. The consumer price figure it cites is the CPI-U index, which rose from 290.9 in December 2021 to 326.0 in December 2025. The 4% projected rise for 2026 is therefore slower than the 12% rise in 2025 but still above zero, so premiums are expected to keep climbing, only more slowly.

How the figures are built

Insurify's methodology matters for interpreting the numbers. It uses its own database of quotes from partner insurers, rate filings collected by Quadrant Information Services, which are weighted by county population, and loss ratio data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners for the projections. The standard policy is the median cost of an HO-3 policy at each state's average dwelling coverage, with liability coverage set at 75% of the dwelling amount. It assumes deductibles of 5% for wind and hurricane, 2% for hail and $1,000 for other claims, and a single-family frame house owned by a person with good credit and no claims in the past five years. Dwelling coverage ranges from about $292,000 in Oklahoma to $500,000 in Hawaii. The company says it updated its methodology in 2026 to reflect dwelling coverage values and peril-specific deductibles. Its projection approach is based on the historical relationship between industry loss ratios and later rate changes. Because it models a particular type of homeowner, a household with an older roof, a claims history or a higher-risk location may see a different result.

The most and least expensive states

Florida is projected to remain the most expensive state at $8,458, an increase of 2%. That is more than double the national average, and follows an 18% rise in 2025 to $8,292. Oklahoma is next at $5,205, up 5%, and Insurify expects it to pass Louisiana, which is projected at $5,035 with no change. Nebraska is projected at $4,560, up 13%, and Texas at $4,529, up 3%. At the other end, Vermont has the lowest projected average at $1,094, up 1%, followed by Maine at $1,359, Utah at $1,370 and Alaska at $1,482. The most expensive counties in 2025 were all in Florida: Monroe at $22,436, Miami-Dade at $15,715 and Palm Beach at $14,235.

Where increases are largest

California is projected to have the largest percentage increase in 2026, at 16%, or $388, to an average of $2,843. Insurify says regulatory limits make increases above that unlikely, and it notes that the state's FAIR Plan, the insurer of last resort, has nearly 600,000 policyholders and a pending request that averages a 36% increase. Nebraska has the largest dollar increase at $532, or 13%. Other large projected increases are New Mexico at 11% ($246), Georgia at 10% ($288), South Carolina at 9% ($278), and Missouri and Arkansas at 7% each. Insurify expects 45 states and Washington, D.C. to see increases; Hawaii and Massachusetts are projected to fall by 2%, Maine by 1%, and Louisiana and Rhode Island are roughly flat.

For 2025, the largest percentage increases were in Minnesota at 34%, Colorado at 33%, Iowa at 28%, Nebraska at 25% and Oklahoma at 24%. North Carolina had the largest decline at 6%, and five states fell or stayed flat. The 25 most expensive states rose 14% in 2025, against 5% in the 25 cheapest.

What Insurify says is driving prices

Insurify points to four factors. Severe convective storms, which produce hail, tornadoes and damaging winds, caused more than $52 billion of insured losses in 2025, the third-highest total on record, with 19 events each causing more than $1 billion in insurer losses. The Los Angeles County wildfires caused $62 billion in economic damage, which it calls the costliest non-hurricane disaster in US history. Building material prices rose 15% in the past year, and because premiums are tied largely to rebuilding costs, that feeds into prices. Insurers are also shifting risk to policyholders through separate hurricane deductibles, typically 5% of dwelling coverage, and actual cash value roof coverage in hail-prone areas. In Florida, Insurify notes that Citizens Property Insurance policyholders fell from over one million to about 400,000 and that Citizens announced a 9% average rate cut.

It also notes that 2025 was the first year in a decade without a US landfalling hurricane, and warns that an active 2026 season could push premiums higher in 2027.

How to read the projections

Three cautions apply. First, the figures are projections from one company, and actual 2026 premiums may differ. Second, averages for a standardized policy do not describe what individual households pay, particularly in states where deductibles and coverage choices vary. Third, a list of 45 states with increases hides large differences: the gap between Vermont and Florida is about $7,364, calculated here, or a factor of more than seven. Because deductibles and exclusions vary, comparing premiums alone can be misleading.

What to watch

Readers can watch for regulator decisions on the California FAIR Plan request, how the 2026 hurricane season develops, and whether building costs keep rising. This article is a summary of one company's published analysis and is not insurance advice.

key_points: Insurify projects the national average home insurance premium will reach $3,057 by the end of 2026, up 4% from $2,948 in 2025, which would be the fifth consecutive year of increases.
The 2025 average was up 12% from $2,636 at the end of 2024, and Insurify says premiums have risen 46% since 2021, about three times the 16% rise in inflation.
Florida is projected to be the most expensive state at $8,458, followed by Oklahoma at $5,205, Louisiana at $5,035, Nebraska at $4,560 and Texas at $4,529, while Vermont is the cheapest at $1,094.
California is projected to see the largest percentage increase at 16%, to $2,843, and Nebraska the largest dollar increase at $532, with 45 states and Washington, D.C. expected to see increases.
Insurify cites severe convective storms causing more than $52 billion of insured losses in 2025, the Los Angeles wildfires, and a 15% rise in building material prices over the past year as drivers.
why_it_matters: Home insurance is a required cost for most mortgage borrowers, so rising premiums feed directly into the monthly cost of owning a home. The figures are one company's model-based projections rather than official statistics, and the state-by-state differences are large enough that national averages say little about any one household.

title: FCA Annual Report Credits an International Finfluencer Crackdown With 3 Arrests and 650 Takedown Requests, as Insider-Dealing Cases Bring 11 Years in Prison Combined
summary: The FCA's Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, published July 9, 2026, describes a nine-regulator finfluencer week of action that produced 3 arrests, 6 criminal proceedings, 11 warning letters, 50 warning list alerts and 650 social media takedown requests, alongside 17 criminal convictions, £1.77 million of market abuse fines and 2,329 scam warnings.
description:
The UK Financial Conduct Authority published its Annual Report and Accounts for 2025/26 and an accompanying press release on July 9, 2026; the web page's metadata lists July 8 as its creation date. The report covers the first year of the FCA's five-year strategy. This article uses the press release. Its headline numbers are the FCA's own claims, and the press release summarises the report rather than reproducing it, so readers who want the methodology behind estimates such as the £5.6 billion benefit figure should consult the annual report itself. The finfluencer action described below took place in June 2025, within the year the report covers.

The finfluencer week of action

Finfluencers are social media personalities who promote financial products or services. In the UK, financial promotions generally must be made or approved by an authorised firm, and a promotion by an unauthorised person can be illegal. According to the press release, the FCA led a week of action in June 2025 in which nine international regulators took part. The results it reports are:

3 arrests;
6 criminal proceedings;
11 targeted warning or cease-and-desist letters;
50 warning list alerts; and
650 requests to social media platforms to take content down.

The release does not say how many of the takedown requests led to content being removed, who was arrested or what the proceedings concern, so this article does not go further. Calculated here, the numbers show that most of the activity was on the content side: 650 takedown requests against 3 arrests.

Insider dealing, fraud and money laundering

The press release headlines insider dealing, saying that two cases secured a combined 11 years in prison. It describes the sentences as covering insider dealing and money laundering. Across the year, the FCA reports 17 criminal convictions, including for fraud, insider dealing, money laundering and offences under the Data Protection Act. It also reports that 12 individuals were fined a combined £1.77 million for market abuse. Dividing, calculated here, gives an average of about £148,000 per individual, though the release does not give the individual amounts, so the average hides large variation.

Firms were also penalised. The FCA fined firms about £14.4 million for transaction reporting failures and control weaknesses, and it fined Barclays £42 million for anti-money-laundering failures. The FCA reports that customers removed as money mules rose 4.4% to 222,173, across 35 firms.

Warnings

The FCA issued 2,329 warnings about unauthorised or potentially scam firms in 2025, up from 2,240 in 2024, an increase of about 4% calculated here. Its Firm Checker tool, launched in January 2025, has been used more than 1.9 million times. The release says firm warning messages protected an average of 694 consumers each week, a 49% increase after a 2026 advertising campaign.

Other claims in the report

The press release lists other results. The FCA estimates that its work delivered £5.6 billion in benefits to consumers, firms and the wider economy. It estimates that Consumer Duty fair-value rules will save people who pay insurance premiums monthly around £157 million a year. It says mortgage reforms are expected to let borrowers access up to £30,000 more, and that final rules on pensions and investments are expected to benefit at least 18 million consumers over the next decade. It reports that final Buy Now Pay Later rules were issued ahead of the regime starting in July 2026.

On growth and efficiency, the FCA reports nearly 50 pro-growth measures delivered in 2025, 132 applications to its AI-supercharged regulatory sandbox, two firms approved under the PISCES private markets framework with two more in the pipeline, new offices in the United States, Asia-Pacific and Singapore, and the retirement of outdated reporting returns, saving £16 million a year in reporting costs. It says AI automation cut handling time for simpler cases from up to four hours to about six minutes.

These are forward-looking estimates and self-reported efficiency figures, and the press release does not provide independent verification.

Quotes

FCA chair Ashley Alder said the regulator had made a strong start to its five-year strategy. Chief executive Nikhil Rathi said there was more to do but that this was a solid foundation.

What it means for consumers and creators

For consumers, the practical lessons are to check whether a firm is authorised using the FCA's Firm Checker, to be wary of financial tips on social media, and to check the FCA's warning list. For people who create financial content, the figures show that arrests and criminal proceedings are possible for illegal promotions, not only warnings. The release does not set out what promotions are permitted, and creators should check the FCA's financial promotion rules. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (press release: FCA cracks down on illegal promotions and market abuse in first year of new strategy, July 9, 2026)
image_alt: Smartphone showing social media apps representing finfluencer promotions (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA published its Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26 on July 9, 2026, covering the first year of its five-year strategy, and estimates its work delivered £5.6 billion in benefits to consumers, firms and the wider economy.

The finfluencer 'week of action' in June 2025 involved nine international regulators and produced 3 arrests, 6 criminal proceedings, 11 targeted warning or cease-and-desist letters, 50 warning list alerts and 650 social media takedown requests.

The FCA secured 17 criminal convictions, including for fraud, insider dealing, money laundering and DPA offences, and two insider-dealing cases led to a combined 11 years in prison; 12 individuals were fined a combined £1.77 million for market abuse.
The FCA issued 2,329 warnings about unauthorised or potentially scam firms in 2025, up from 2,240 in 2024, and fined Barclays £42 million for anti-money-laundering failures.
The report also cites Firm Checker used over 1.9 million times, and the FCA's own estimate that Consumer Duty fair-value rules save monthly insurance premium payers about £157 million a year.
why_it_matters: Social media is now a main route by which younger investors meet financial products, and unauthorised promotions can lead to scams or unsuitable investments. The figures show how the FCA is using arrests, warning lists and takedowns alongside traditional enforcement, which tells consumers and influencers where the line is drawn.
